questions.q: What does a feature flag separate?
questions.explain: With a flag, new code goes to production switched off (deploy). You switch it on later, for a few users first (release). If something breaks, you switch it off in seconds, without another deploy.
options: The frontend from the backend
Deploying the code from releasing the feature to users
Tests from production code
Free users from paying users, as a permission check

questions.q: Which of these is not one of the flag uses the lesson describes?
questions.explain: A flag says whether a feature is switched on. Whether a user may do something is a permission check, which you keep from the permissions lesson.
options: A gradual release to more and more users
A kill switch that turns off a feature causing trouble
An A/B test that shows two versions to two groups
Deciding whether a user is allowed to delete another user's task

questions.q: In @zudojs/feature-flags, what is a provider?
questions.explain: createFeatureFlags reads definitions from a provider and answers questions. createMemoryProvider keeps them in memory; a real system reads them from a database or a flag service.
options: The user who asks for a flag
The place where the flag definitions are stored, such as memory, a database or a flag service
A rule that turns a flag on for some users
The npm package that sends flags to the browser

questions.q: A flag has several rules. How is the value chosen?
questions.explain: Order matters: put the most specific rule first, like the staff or beta list, and the broad rules, like a percentage, after it.
options: All matching rules are combined
The last matching rule wins
Rules are checked in order; the first one that matches wins, and if none matches the default is served
A random matching rule is used

questions.q: Where should the Task API get the plan attribute for the evaluation context?
questions.explain: Anything the client sends can be changed by the client. If plan came from the body or a header, anyone could send "pro" and get pro features for free.
options: From the request body, where the client sends "plan": "pro"
From an x-plan header
From the verified logged-in user and your database
From a query parameter, so it is easy to test

questions.q: An admin-panel flag is on for users with role: "admin". What else does the admin route need?
questions.explain: A flag is not a permission. Keep the permission check from the permissions lesson on the server, and read the role from your own authentication, never from a header.
options: Nothing: the flag already checks the role
The normal permission check; a flag says a feature is on, not that this user may use it
A second flag with the same rule
A visibility: "client" setting on the flag

questions.q: Why is a percentage rollout deterministic instead of random?
questions.explain: If the answer were random, a feature could appear and vanish on every page load. The rule hashes the flag key and the user id into one of 10,000 buckets, so the same user always lands in the same bucket.
options: Random numbers are too slow in JavaScript
A user who saw the feature must still see it after a reload
So that every user gets the feature at the same time
So the server can skip the rules

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The bucket comes from a hash of the flag key and the user id, so the same pair always gives the same bucket, a number from 0 to 9,999.
options: true true
false true
true false
false false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 0% reaches nobody and 100% reaches everybody. Between them, a percentage reaches about that share of users.

questions.q: You raise a rollout from 20% to 50%. What does this print?
questions.explain: A user is inside when their bucket is below the percentage. Raising the percentage only adds buckets, so everybody who already had the feature keeps it.
options: true
false

questions.q: The flag key is part of the hash, not only the user id. Why?
questions.explain: With the key in the hash, each flag spreads users differently. Otherwise the same unlucky users would be first in line for every new feature.
options: So the bucket changes on every request
So the same 20% of users do not end up in every experiment
So users can pick their own bucket
Because user ids can be empty

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A context without userId, tenantId or sessionId counts as the single user "anonymous", so every anonymous visitor gets the same answer. Give logged-out visitors a session id if they should be spread out.

questions.q: How do you learn which sorting variant wins the A/B test?
questions.explain: A variant label has only two values, so it is safe as a metric label. Comparing completed tasks per variant shows which version works better.
options: Ask the users which group they are in
Record the variant with what the user did, for example a tasks.completed metric with a variant label
Add a userId label to the metric
Look at which variant has the higher weight

questions.q: The file storage is failing, so you switch off the number flag upload-limit-mb with enabled: false. Which definition really stops uploads?
questions.explain: A disabled flag ignores its rules and serves its off value. A boolean flag's off value is false, but a number flag has no natural "off", so without offValue it serves its defaultValue: 50 MB uploads are still allowed. offValue: 0 makes switching it off really stop uploads.
options: { key: "upload-limit-mb", enabled: false, defaultValue: 50 }
{ key: "upload-limit-mb", enabled: false, defaultValue: 50, offValue: 0 }
{ key: "upload-limit-mb", enabled: false, defaultValue: 50, rules: [{ type: "static", value: 0 }] }
{ key: "upload-limit-mb", enabled: false, defaultValue: 50, metadata: { expiresAt: new Date("2020-01-01") } }

questions.q: The mail provider is down, and every task completion fails while sending an email. What does a kill switch give you?
questions.explain: One change to the flag stops the failing optional work. The core feature, completing tasks, keeps working.
options: A way to retry the emails faster
Turn emails off in seconds, without a deploy, while tasks can still be completed
A way to hide the error from the logs
An automatic switch to another mail provider

questions.q: What does "fail closed" mean for feature flags?
questions.explain: An unreachable flag store must never switch a feature on. The safe answer is "off", and the failure is reported to onError.
options: When the flag store fails, turn every flag on so users are not blocked
When in doubt (disabled, expired or unreachable flag), the feature is off
Close the server when the flag store fails
Close the browser tab of users without flags

questions.q: The flag store is down. What does this print?
questions.explain: isEnabled fails closed: false. getBoolean(key, fallback) serves your fallback, here true. After the first failure the instance leaves the provider alone for 5 seconds, so onError received one error, not two.
options:
false
true
[ 'flag service unreachable' ]

true

questions.q: When is getBoolean(key, true) a good choice?
questions.explain: The fallback is used when the flag is missing or unreachable. Use true only for features that are safe to keep on; everything new should fall back to off.
options: For a new beta feature
For a payment change that is still being tested
For a feature that every user already has and that is safe to keep running, like task export
For every flag, so users are never blocked

questions.q: What should the Task API do in onError?
questions.explain: The flags already fail closed, so the request can continue. But someone must learn that the flag store is down, and the log is where they look.
options: Throw, so the request fails
Log the problem, so you notice the flag store is failing
Switch every flag on
Nothing: errors are handled already

questions.q: Why does a snapshot include only flags marked visibility: "client"?
questions.explain: A snapshot sends evaluated values to the browser, and only for flags you chose. Rules and other flags stay on the server, so the client cannot see who else is on the beta list.
options: Other flags are too big to send
Flag definitions can reveal unannounced plans or the names of beta customers
The browser cannot read boolean values
Server flags are always off

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: linus is not on the user list, so task-comments is false for him. acme-migration has no visibility: "client", so it stays on the server.
options: {"task-comments":false,"dark-mode":true}
{"task-comments":true,"dark-mode":true}
{"task-comments":false,"dark-mode":true,"acme-migration":false}
{"dark-mode":true}

questions.q: The browser received {"task-comments": true} in its snapshot. What must the server still do when the user posts a comment?
questions.explain: Use the snapshot to decide what to show. Anything in the browser can be edited, so every action is checked again on the server.
options: Nothing: the snapshot came from the server
Check the flag (and the permission) again on the server, because the user can change anything in their browser
Ask the browser to send the snapshot back and trust it
Check only that the request has a comment body

questions.q: Why does the Task API keep all flags in one file with an owner and an expiresAt date?
questions.explain: When a feature is fully rolled out, delete the flag and its if. The owner and date make it clear who should do that and when.
options: The package refuses flags without them
So old flags get removed; a forgotten flag becomes an if nobody dares to delete
So the browser can see who owns each flag
So the flag turns on by itself at that date

questions.q: Today is after the expiresAt date. What does this print?
questions.explain: After its expiresAt date, a flag ignores its rules and serves its off value with the reason expired. For a boolean flag that is false, so the feature switches off and somebody notices the forgotten flag.
options: false expired
true static
true expired
false default

questions.q: What does flags.close() do when the app shuts down?
questions.explain: The flags instance listens to the provider so it sees changes at once. close() stops that listener, so the process can shut down cleanly.
options: It deletes all flags from the provider
It switches every flag off
It stops listening to the provider's change announcements
It sends a snapshot to every browser

questions.q: A flag rule checks { type: "attribute", attribute: "role", operator: "equals", value: "admin" }, and the Task API fills role from a request header. What is wrong?
questions.explain: It is unsafe twice. The role must come from your verified authentication, and admin actions still need the real permission check on the server.
options: Nothing, as long as the header is lower-case
The client controls the header, so anyone can become "admin"; and a flag must not replace the permission check
Attribute rules cannot compare strings
Only the in operator works for roles

questions.q: Add a rule to task-comments so it is on for the users ada and grace only. The program should print true true false.
questions.explain: A user rule lists user ids and the value to serve. Everyone else gets the safe default false.

questions.q: Add an attribute rule so new-editor is on for users whose email attribute ends with @taskapi.dev. The program should print true false.
questions.explain: An attribute rule compares one attribute with an operator. Without a result, a match serves true.

questions.q: Add a rule so page-size is 100 for the plans pro and team, and stays 20 for everyone else. The program should print 20 100 100.
questions.explain: The in operator matches one of several values, and result sets the value a match serves. A flag value can be a number, not only a boolean.

questions.q: Write the emails definition as a safe kill switch: on while enabled, and off after it is disabled. Use a safe defaultValue and a rule that switches it on. The program should print true false.
questions.explain: defaultValue: false plus a static rule that serves true. The feature is on while the flag is enabled, and every failure path (disabled, deleted, unreachable) leads to off.

questions.q: Finish contextFor(user, body): build the evaluation context from the verified user only (userId and the plan attribute). Ignore the request body, whose plan the client can set to anything. The program should print 100 20.
questions.explain: The body is written by the client, so its plan proves nothing. The verified users say ada is on pro (100) and alan is on free (20), whatever their bodies claim.

questions.q: Finish clientFlags(context): take flags.snapshot(context) (a Map from key to result) and return a plain object from each key to its value. The program should print {"task-comments":true,"dark-mode":true}.
questions.explain: The client gets values, not rules. Only visibility: "client" flags are in the snapshot, so acme-migration stays on the server.

questions.q: Finish countInside(percentage): count how many of the users user-0 to user-999 are inside the task-comments rollout, using isInRollout(key, userId, percentage). The program should print 0 1000 true.
questions.explain: A 20% rollout reaches about 200 of 1000 users, not exactly 200, because each user's bucket comes from a hash. 0% reaches nobody and 100% everybody.

questions.q: The flag store is down. Add an onError option that pushes error.message into problems, so the failure can be logged. The program should print false [ 'flag service unreachable' ].
questions.explain: The flag fails closed (false), and the failure reaches onError. In the Task API you would log it there, so someone notices the flag store is down.

questions.q:
Finish complete(userId, id): ask flags.isEnabled("task-emails", { userId }) and return task <id> done, email sent when it is on, or task <id> done, email skipped when it is off. The program should print:

task 1 done, email sent
task 1 done, email skipped
questions.explain: Ask the flag before the optional work. When the kill switch is flipped, the task is still completed; only the email is skipped.
questions.expected:
task 1 done, email sent
task 1 done, email skipped

questions.q: Finish groupSizes(count): evaluate task-sorting for the users user-0 to user-(count-1) and count how many get each value in a Map. Then the program checks that both groups exist and that the sizes add up. It should print 2 true.
questions.explain: Each user lands in one of the two named groups, about half in each. Record the variant with what users do to learn which version wins.
